speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RESIGNATION OF CONTROLLER-APPOINTMENT OF SUCCESSOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Press dispatches from Vancouver this morning indicate that there is to be some change in the timber control. Could the minister make a statement on that?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: RESIGNATION OF CONTROLLER-APPOINTMENT OF SUCCESSOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the report has just been called to my attention. It is a fact that Mr. David Rosenberry, who has been associated with timber control for the past six years, has tendered his resignation, to take effect on August 15. He has been suffering from overwork for some time and felt that he must be relieved so that he could take a prolonged holiday before returning to his private business. Consideration is being given to his successor, and the most suitable man seems to be the present coordinator of housing, Mr. Terrence Flahiff. It is the present intention to recommend Mr. Flahiff to succeed Mr. Rosenberry.

speechtext: There is one other question I should like to direct to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, because I believe he is in charge of the department concerned. It has to do with reports in the Montreal Star of yesterday with regard to the dumping of shoes, which is still unexplained, and also the destruction of a quantity of khaki and blue shirts, towels, et cetera. Will the minister have an investigation made into this matter, in view of the fact that there have been so many reports of destruction of necessary goods when they are in short supply? Also will consideration be given to setting up a commission to look into the matter, particularly to report on the dumping of shoes?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO DISCARDING OF SHOES AND SLIPPERS-SHIRTS, TOWELS, ETC.
speechtext:
A most exhaustive investigation was instituted into the ques-

tion of shoes, and it was found that the allegations that were made of destruction of usable property by War Assets Corporation are wholly without foundation. We invited the reporters to visit the plant at Valleyfield at any time they cared to do so without notice, and I understand the Star reporter did visit the plant with photographers yesterday. I expect that Monday's Star will give the results of his investigation. He was given authority to make a most complete investigation on his own. I can assure my hon. friend that since the first allegations were made, every service of the government has investigated the situation from its point of view at Valleyfield and at the point of shipment of the materials. War Assets Corporation have made a thorough investigation and I can assure my hon. friend that the allegations of destruction of valuable property are wholly without foundation.
As to the shirts, so far as we can find out that report is based entirely on gossip. We have found that no usable shirts have been sold as scrap material by War Assets Corporation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL COMMISSIONERS, TRANSFER OF CERTAIN JURISDICTION, AND GRANTING OF MONEY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, August 9, consideration in committee of bill No. 357, to amend the Federal District Commission Act-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-National capital district.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice):	Mr. Chairman, it is not my
intention at this time, or perhaps at any time, to make any lengthy plea in favour of the 63260-289J
provisions for the improvement of the federal area. This bill is nothing new; it is simply a continuation of provisions that have been made for almost the last fifty years in that regard. The fact that the matter had been in progress for fifty years should not surprise anyone. I should be very much surprised, and my descendants would be very much disappointed, I am sure, if it did not go on for more than fifty years in the future. I think' it is the fairly general view that the development of the national capital will keep pace with the development of the country as a nation, and I hope that will go on for a very long time.
The leader of th# opposition asked me at the resolution stage if I would make a brief statement on the historical, background of this movement, which is not the policy of any one party but is something to which all those who have had responsibility for government in Canada over the last half century have been giving careful, sympathetic and effective consideration and cooperation.
The historical background of the commission is given on pages 60 and 61 in No. 3 of the proceedings of the joint committee of the senate and the House of Commons, reports ing its sittings of Wednesday, June 28, 1944. I mention this because it is given in greater detail than I propose to give it in summarizing it this morning. But perhaps for the immediate information of hon. members who may not have this report at hand just at the moment, I may say that the federal district commission had its inception as the Ottawa improvement commission in 1899. It was established for the purpose of beautifying and improving the city of Ottawa as the capital of Canada by the construction of parks, driveways, public squares, boulevards and so forth.
Four commissioners comprised its membership, three being appointed by the governor in council and the fourth by the city of Ottawa. The chairman was named by the governor in council. All were to serve without remuneration. An annual grant of 860,000 was provided for a period of ten years from July 1, 1899. By an amending act assented to on August 13, 1903 the period during which the annual grant of $60,000 was to be paid was extended to twenty years, from the first of July, 1899 and the commission was given power to borrow up to $250,000 by the sale of debentures.
By an amending act assented to on May 4, 1910 the annual grant was increased to $100,000 for a ten-year period commencing July 1, 1909. An act to consolidate and amend the acts respecting the Ottawa improvement commission was then assented to on July 17,
Federal District Commission

1919. These dates will indicate that it was a matter that was being dealt with not only by one party but by whatever administration had responsibility for the affairs of the country.
The act of 1919 increased the annual grant to $150,000 for a ten-year period from July 1, 1919, and then in 1,927 the name of the commission was changed from the Ottawa improvement commission to the federal distiet *commission. The act passed in that year increased the powers of the commission to enable it to extend its activities to areas or districts outside the capital proper, and provided for the appointment of a commissioner .as a representative of the city of Hull. The dominion government, I^m told, was actuated by the desire to widen the scope of the commission's functions to embrace not only Ottawa and the immediate vicinity but Hull and the adjoining municipalities on both sides as an integral part of the national capital area.
The act of 1927 also increased the annual grant of the commission to $250,000, but this was reduced again to $200,000 in 1928 when provision was made for a grant of $3,000,000 to be expended upon capital improvements over a period of years. The beautification and improvement works which had been commenced in 1900 for Ottawa and district, under these authorizing acts of parliament, consist of parks, landscapes, driveways, the latter extending from Rockcliffe park east of the city of Ottawa to Aylmer road west of the city of Hull, The driveway follows as closely as convenient the banks of the Ottawa and Rideau rivers and the Rideau canal. Approximately twenty-two miles of driveways have been constructed, Gatineau park, comprising
16,000	acres situated in the Laurentian hills on the Quebec side of the river, about seven air miles northwest of Ottawa, is being preserved in its natural state of wooded hills, valleys, lakes and streams, for the enjoyment of the public.
By orders in council the responsibility of improving and maintaining, the grounds of Rideau Hall, those surrounding the national research council buildings and other dominion government buildings in Ottawa was transferred from the Department of Public Works to the commission in the years 1932 to 1934. Amounts for this work are voted annually by parliament in estimates approved by the governor in council.
The number of properties now serviced by the commission is 110. The land now owned or controlled by the federal district commission in and around Ottawa, exclusive of the 16,000-acre national park, is:	Owned by the
federal district commission, 758 acres; leased from the crown, 224 acres; leased from
£Mr. St. Laurent.!
the city of Ottawa and developed and maintained by the commission, 129 acres; grounds of government buildings maintained through the instrumentality of the commission under these orders in council, about 200 acres, or a total of grounds thus administered and maintained by the commission in Ottawa and the immediate vicinity of 1,311 acres. In addition, as I stated a moment ago, there is the 16,000 acres of land in the Gatineau park.
The leader of the opposition in his inquiry the other day, seemed particularly interested in having a statement of receipts and expenditures of the commission since its inception. The figures I have been given are as follows:
Statutory grants from 1899 to 1909,
$60,000 a year for 10 years	 $600,000
Statutory grants from 1909 to 1919,
$100,000 a year for 10 years		1,000,000
Statutory grants from 1919 to 1927,
$150,000 a year for 8 years	 1,200,000
Statutory grants from 1927 to 1928,
1 year	 250,000
Statutory grants from 1928 to 1946,
$200,000 a year for 18 years		3,600,000
In addition thereto, special grant
made under the act of 1928	 3,000,000
Grand total	 $9,650,000
In addition to that there have been votes by parliament over that period of $1,162,788. There have also been advances from government departments for work on the maintenance of grounds and new buildings of $2,016,766, making a grand total of $12,829,554 over the forty-eight years.
I come now to the expenditures for that period: For the construction and maintenance of the parkway system, $10,690,117; for the maintenance of grounds of government buildings, $1,375,125; for the development of grounds of new government buildings, $641,640.
In connection with the future work of the commission there are a few points I should like to mention. First of all I wish to point out that there is no provision in this bill or in anything parliament is being asked to pass making this a national war memorial. This is a bill to amend the act respecting the federal district commission, and these amendments are required, and I trust will be made by the house, entirely apart from any idea as to whether or not the development of the national capital should be classified as a national war memorial. I know that the Prime Minister has urged that the development of the national capital might be a fitting way for the nation to express its gratification at the role played by the Canadian nation in the last war. That is a matter about which it was apparent from the debate last evening

Federal District Commission
that there is no unanimity of opinion, and it is not my purpose to ask the house to make any pronouncement about it at this time.
This bill is for the continuation of the development of the capital area consisting of Ottawa and the surrounding district. I think there is much to be said for the view that it is something that the Canadian nation would wish to do entirely regardless of any other consideration. I think it is something that the Canadian nation feels should keep pace with the development of the country. The appropriation suggested at this time would not be required, and would probably not be justified, if we in this house felt that the Canadian nation had reached the full stage of its national development and of its importance in world affairs. But as the nation develops-and I think we all feel that it will develop for a long period still, and that this immense area of the habitable portion of the globe is to be the home of a much larger population than the twelve million people who control it at the present time-as that goes on, it will be necessary that the national capital keep pace with the development of the nation. In order that that may be possible I think it is only the part of prudence and foresight to lay out plans which will not be carried out at any early day but which it would be possible to realize without having to destroy too much placed in the way of their realization when the proper time comes. It was for that purpose, and it is for the same purpose, that these capital sums are being asked parliament to appropriate. There are a great many places in Canada where the development has been such that it has necessitated the tearing down of things which would still intrinsically have had some value but which had to make way for something more useful which the developments had made necessary.
As I said at the resolution stage, the work will be somewhat greater in extent than it had been, hitherto, because of two factors. One is that over the past five or six years the development of our people as a nation has proceeded with greater rapidity than it had at any previous period. Canada's position as one of the nations of the world has asserted itself to a much greater degree during the last few years than had happened at any time before, though it must be at once stated that the groundwork for that development and for that expansion had been laid from the very beginning. This is just one example of what I have in mind. The exchange of diplomatic representatives between the Canadian government and the other governments has brought to Ottawa a large body of officials representing other nations of the world. Their presence in Ottawa has put some strain upon the buildings, upon the layout which had previously sufficed for the requirements of the business transacted on behalf of the nation at the national capital, and that is still going on.
The second factor which makes it appear desirable to proceed a little more rapidly is that so much of the maintenance and development work had to give way to more urgent matters during the war period, and they had to be deferred until this time. The federal district commission is like any other large body in Canada. It had to allow activities that were not of vital necessity to win the war to be deferred until the war had been won.
This bill does not deal with any general plan of development which may be decided on for the capital, and I would not expect that there would be any decision made at this time or in the immediate future blueprinting what was to be done and at what dates it would be done. But a general over-all plan is being prepared which would make possible the development of a national capital with a population two or three times what it is at the present time, showing what a city of that size as the national capital would be apt to require. It is suggested in this bill that there be such cooperation between the various authorities concerned as would prevent the doing of things which would be obstacles to the realization of that larger plan, as and when conditions made it proper to develop it.
To cover expenditures of a capital type, such as those for the purchase of lands and works, the development of the parkway system and so on, the bill before the house provides that over a period of years the sum of $3,000,000 may be allocated to the commission, as a similar sum of $3,000,000 was made available between 1928 and 1935 under the terms of the 1928 act. To cover the increased current expenditures an increase in the annual grant from $200,000 to $300,000 is also requested.
The part of the work of the commission which will be connected with the broader developments of the capital will require special arrangements. As hon. members know, the government has had Mr. Jacques Greber to advise on the general planning. I was much interested and impressed by what was said last evening by the hon. member for Eglinton. I think all Canadians wish this capital to be expressive of Canadian mentality and Canadian conditions, that it be the capital of the Canadian nation and not a pocket edition of anything already in existence else-
Federal District Commission

where. But as the hon. member suggested, in that connection it is wise to have advice as good as can be obtained, and I think the knowledge a competent landscape or town development architect has acquired over a long period of years in examining the layout of other capitals or other cities is something which can be of considerable assistance. I do not suppose there is a city in the world where mistakes have not been made. I think it wise to have the advice of one who has studied the situation elsewhere, who knows what mistakes it is necessary to guard against and who can suggest outlines and general plans to be worked out in the atmosphere of a Canadian mentality and of Canadian conditions in this federal area. I have been here only a few years and am not competent to express any views, but I am not convinced that the development of the railway terminal here has not been a mistake to a certain degree, and that it might not have been wiser and more helpful to the ultimate development of a greater federal capital to have made some other arrangements for bringing the railway systems into the city. I am not expressing that as a definite opinion, but there are those who are not convinced that some mistake was not made there.
The work 'being prepared under the guidance of Mr. Greber is being done here in Canada by a staff of Canadian architects and draftsmen, and is something that will make available not a plan for immediate realization but a plan which will show what kind of arrangements it would appear in the light of experience to be necessary to provide for in a national capital that might have two or three times or perhaps even more the population of present day Ottawa.

In the report made by the committee the government was authorized to ask the federal district commission to call the railways together with regard to a new union station and also with regard to the elimination of their tracks. I was wondering if that authorization had been carried out.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That matter is under consideration, and I was about to state to the committee what has been done in that connection. Last December the matter was quite fully gone into and a tentative decision arrived at to set up three committees, one to be known as a national planning ccqmmittee, the second to be known as a parks committee and the third to be known as a railway committee. The national planning committee I understand has been authorized and would consist of seventeen members comprising the mayors of both Ottawa and Hull, with the
[Mr. St. Laurent.!
other members to be appointed by the federal district commission, not necessarily chosen only from among their own members, to advise on the acceptance or otherwise of this general plan as something to work to in future years. Some of the members are to be well qualified in the science and practice of town planning and to be chosen, because of the necessity for frequent meetings, largely from the cities of Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto. They are to be appointed by the federal district commission under authority of order in council P.C. 5634 of August 16, 1945. As I said, two of them are to be the mayors of Ottawa and Hull. The personnel of this committee is to serve on an honorary basis, getting only the reasonable out of pocket expenses incurred in attending meetings. I may add that from the outset the whole of the work that has been done by this Ottawa improvement commission, or the federal district commission, has been done entirely without remuneration, as a voluntary and very willing contribution of public-minded citizens.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL COMMISSIONERS, TRANSFER OF CERTAIN JURISDICTION, AND GRANTING OF MONEY
speechtext:
A work of love.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: A work of love, to provide for the future generations of Canadians. The principal function of this national planning committee will be to meet as often as required for the purpose of laying down the broad general outline of the master plan for the capital district, with Mr. Greber acting in the capacity of a consultant, a capacity which I understood the hon. member for Eglinton to favour in his address last evening. The actual work is being done at the expense of the federal district commission by a staff which I understand now consists of thirteen members, architects, draftsmen and so forth, working under the general direction of Mr. Greber. This national planning committee will report to the government through the commission and will advise the commission as to the subsequent and gradual development of the general scheme, as and when conditions appear to make it opportune to undertake it.
The second committee which has not yet been formally set up by by-law of the federal district commission, but which is under consideration. could not operate effectively it was felt, until the general plan was available. This parks committee would have a membership of five persons chosen by the federal district commission from the federal capital area, persons who have in particular displayed a keen interest in the formation and development of Gatineau park. Its chief duty would be to advise as to the management and further development of Gatineau park and

Federal District Commission
other park areas, from the point of view of the maximum use the public could make of those facilities.
The third committee would be the railways committee. It was felt that there again there must be this general master plan as a thing to work to in the future before the railway committee could do any valuable or effective work toward the solution of that part of the problem. After the national planning committee have determined the extent of the changes which would ultimately be required in the railway lines in and around Ottawa, in order to conform with the requirements of a much larger capital city and development this committee would work out the details and the cost of such changes. I anticipate that would be something which it would be very important to have carefully gone into.
We have heard the old saying that Rome was not built in- a day. I do not think the capital of Canada is going to be built in a day. I do believe that no matter how desirable certain things might appear to be, they will have to wait until the opportune time-until they can be undertaken without putting any undue burden upon the economy of the nation.
This railways committee will be appointed by the federal district commission and will consist of the chosen representatives of the railway companies, representatives of Ottawa and Hull and also of the board of transport commissioners.
Before concluding these remarks I wish to say a word about the interesting and useful suggestion by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid1) and the remarks and comments made upon it by other hon. members. I think everyone is in agreement that this federal area should be regarded as a thing of interest not only to the citizens of Ottawa and Hull but to the citizens of Canada generally.
The bill does propose that of a commission of fifteen members, at least five-and the number has not been limited to five-would be chosen as representing not the residents of the capital area but the residents of the rest of Canada. It would1 be possible, even with a commission of fifteen, to have a representative from each of the nine provinces. The object the government had in view in submitting the bill as it now stands was to have the Canadian public generally represented in this body.
If it is the feeling of the house that there should be a legislative requirement that at least one member of the commission would be ordinarily resident in each of the nine provinces, it does make the commission a little more unwieldly, inasmuch as there would be a commission of nineteen instead of the fifteen
as set out in the bill. But that is not a serious objection. I am sure that if there were a commission of nineteen there would be occasions when routine meetings would be held, at which times the whole nineteen would not feel they had to attend. But when there was anything of major importance they would feel it their dirty to respond.
Of course hon. members realize that as in the past this is going to be asked of them as a labour of love. They are going to be asked to serve without remuneration because they would be chosen by reason of their vision, outlook and public-spiritedness. We felt we might achieve that object by having regional representation. However, if hon. members feel it is preferable to have the nine provinces, as provincial units, separately represented, there will be no objection to accepting an amendment along those lines.
Having made these remarks I suggest that the committee might now be prepared to consider the terms of the legislation proposed. There may be other points which during the course of the discussion hon. members may wish to urge. They may feel sure that there is no desire to force anything upon the country. There is a desire to do what the predecessors of this government, to whatever party they belonged, have been doing for the last halfcentury, and to which I feel sure all future governments, composed of no matter which of the political parties, will also wish to add their respective contributions.

What I mean is that the word "area" is far more appropriate than the word "district". While it is true that this body was first incorporated as the Ottawa improvement commission, it had a title that more fittingly represented its activity then than that of dis-63260-290J
trict commission. For a number of years in this house and in the country at large a great deal of confusion, as well as some antagonism to the aims and objects of the government in the improvement of the federal capital area, has arisen because of the use of the terms "federal district" and "federal district commission."
I do not think the people of Canada are in favour of creating a federal district to be run by a commission with the probable loss of local autonomy. I do not think the people of Canada want to have established a federal area similar to that in Washington, run by commission government. I do not think it makes for harmony or the welfare of the community or of the project itself, when we bear in mind that we are taking in portions of two provinces with different municipalities, two provinces with different, types of law, different laws governing real property, different educational desires, different municipal management and all the rest of it. Under these circumstances I do not think there should be any doubt about our intentions. There should be no loss to the community or to the province of local autonomy.
The commission that has been appointed has acted well as an advisory coordinating committee rather than as a legislative and enacting body. I feel therefore that the word "area" should be substituted for that of "district", and the word "committee" for that of "commission". The minister who is piloting the bill might consider adopting this suggestion, which would assist greatly in furthering the objects we have in view. I think we should change the name from "federal district commission" to "federal area committee". If such a change were made the people of Canada generally and in the area locally would look much more favourably upon this undertaking, and from a more realistic point of view. I am pleased to notice that the minister himself, whether intentionally or accidentally, used the words "federal area" three times in his speech this morning. My hon. friend asked a fit and proper question, because just yesterday, in behalf of the. residents of my own riding, I sought permission to get a bus coming from the suburban, area west of the city to Confederation square, to serve the shoppers, the workers and the people from the west end. I was told that because of the bottleneck on Confederation square a bus service to serve the west end of the city could not be permitted there; they could not be served. In further answer to my hon. friend I would say that Ottawa never sought to have Confederation square as it is. They have always sought and continue to seek to have that congested area improved, but their hands are tied. The difficulty is there. I believe that they have done their best to try to re-route traffic, to try to manage traffic, to try to arrange traffic to create as little congestion as possible. They have gone so far as to place extra policemen in the area in busy hours to guide the traffic. I do not know what else can be done, except to put in a new thoroughfare to take some of the traffic from that bottleneck. Until that is done the authorities of Ottawa are helpless to mitigate in any way the conglomerated traffic conditions on Confederation square. I do not know what can be done other than a new route which will take traffic elsewhere.
Now that parliament is considering the grant of $3 million, one of the most necessary, must urgent and most useful ways of spending some portion of that money is to relieve conditions in that area. The minister has said that the committee on railways and the committee on planning must each await the returns of the greater federal area general scheme. I agree with that in part, but only in a very small part. The general scheme is one of long development. It has been worked on in one form or another for fifteen or twenty years. The report of no committee has ever been accepted by parliament, not even the report made by the Holt committee. Mr. Greber has now been working on it for approximately a year. Coordinating com-

mittees are working on it. Surely the time has long since past when for the sake not only of the city of Ottawa but of everybody who comes to this city and who must pass that area, something should be done about it. I believe I would be doing my duty, not as a citizen of Ottawa but as a citizen of Canada, to urge upon the government the imminent necessity of relieving the situation which prevails there. I have had experience in Ottawa with respect to the building of houses, factories, warehouses and all that kind of thing. Buildings of that type are being held up in so far as planning is concerned until a master plan is produced. Ottawa does not wish to complain about it. We are very glad to wait, but I say in a kindly way that the quicker we can get a guide to the development of the city and the relief of traffic and the establishment of industrial areas and some insight as to when, where and how the railway situation can be improved, the quicker it will be for the development not only of Ottawa but of the federal area.
The highway situation throughout both sections of Ottawa, east and west, is not a happy one. It is not as bad as Confederation square, but if you go through the westerly section of the city you will come to a junction of two or three railways, and you find traffic areas seriously congested. Development of improvements in directing the railways and the directing of traffic in the congested areas all await the master plan. May I therefore, expressing my own opinion, and probably asking the members of the committee to direct their thoughts to it, move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo:
That the Federal District Commission Act, 1927, and this bill, be amended so as to have the words "district commission" wherever they appear in the said act or bill be substituted for the words "area committee."

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. There has been far too much importance attached1 to the use of words. Some seem to have forgotten that a rose would smell the same whatever you called it. All that parliament is being asked to adopt are the provisions on the left-hand pages of the document which is before the committee. There are some who may regard this as a tribute to the effort of Canada during the war which has speeded up this development; but all that is being asked for are the provisions which are set out to become part of the statute, and the explanations, can be accepted or rejected without in any way affecting the purport of the legislation parliament is asked to enact.
I know that the Prime Minister personally feels that the development as rapidly as possible of the national capital might be such a fitting memorial that there might not have to be other forms of memorials, but it is quite evident that that is not by any means a unanimous view. What is asked for here is something that would and should be asked for even had there been no war at all, and it will have to be done whether or not there are other forms of memorials provided as tributes to the gallant men who served the state in the armed forces during the war.
With respect to the amendment proposed by the hon. member, I would ask him if he would not withdraw it at 'this time. This is a matter in which a great many people are interested. The name "federal district commission" is the name under which the property is now held. To change it would involve rewriting another bill to carry out the idea which prompts this amendment, and I would ask the hon. member if he would not withdraw it at this time. It
has been placed before the house and the country. I can assure the hon. gentleman that it will be given consideration, but I do not know enough about the affairs of this commission to feel at all comfortable about taking the responsibility of accepting or definitely turning down 'this suggestion.
This is a long range matter. The name "federal district commission" has been used since 1927, I think. The fact that in the United States there is under the control of the government of that nation a district known asa federal district may have indisposed some toward the aims of this commission. As a matter of fact there is nothing and there never has been, in the statute or in the attitude of the commission, constituting any threat to the local autonomy of the two bodies governing on the two sides of the river here.
I think the hon. member will agree with that. There is nothing and never has been anything in the statute or in the attitude of the members of the commission that implied the slightest threat to the autonomy of the municipal corporations, and I do not think there has been at any time anything done by the commission or any member of it that would make the municipal authorities feel their prerogatives were being trespassed upon; and I am sure that is the present mentality of the commission. It may be that it would be desirable to avoid any suggestion of a possible menace resulting from the similarity of this name with that of the United States commission, but I would be much obliged to my hon. friend if he would just allow the matter to stand as something to be considered at another time, and not insist that a decision be made concerning it at this moment.

Mr. Chairman, I am gratified at the tendency of hon. members not to try to isolate this area from other parts of Canada, or to regard it as something separate from the general interest; because after all Ottawa is the capital of our great land. I think it only natural that we should take pride in having a capital which will be a credit to the country generally, and I believe that is the feeling of the committee, regardless of the details which may sometimes divide us in connection with its beautification.
I suppose the idea of associating this beautification scheme with a national war memorial arose from a movement which has made considerable headway in Canada in the period following World War II, as a result of which in various municipalities and counties throughout Canada something perhaps more material in the way of war memorials is being proposed. In many places community centres seem to have gained great favour. I express no opinion concerning the matter, other than to suggest that we should not go too far in either direction. I believe there is a course which will appeal to most Canadians; and if I may express a personal thought in connection with a national war memorial, I should hope that what is set out in the explanatory note of this bill will not prevent further consideration of the whole matter of a national war memorial on some other basis if in the days to come that should be considered the proper thing to do. This section provides:
(6) In any case where the commission does not give its approval under this section the governor in council may give such approval.
As the minister has stated, I do not think it is probable that the commission will be recommending one thing or opposing one thing

Federal District Commission
and then the privy council take the opposite stand, but I believe in the past there have been occasions on which buildings have been erected in inopportune locations near the federal district driveway and which were not approved of by the commission. It is possible that some of those buildings were erected by the government as well as by private individuals and they have interfered with the proper zoning and the proper intentions of the commission so far as the driveway is concerned. In the case of the dominion government deciding to build a building in a certain location and not being able to get the approval of the federal district commission, this section would give the governor in council the power to pay no attention, as it were, to the federal district commission. But I think this section goes even farther, it gives the governor in council the right to overrule any power which may be given to the federal district commission by section 4, which will be the new section 6A. I think it is desirous that there be a limit upon the power of the governor in council to disregard the commission's findings. Has the minister any particular reason for wanting that there? If the governor in council does overrule the federal district commission, it should be in direct and specific terms rather than by implication or necessity, as it might be here.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If the hon. member reads the section he will find that the bill has not purported to -take away from the municipal authorities their rights with respect to zoning and has not proposed to substitute the authority of the federal district commission for the rights of the local autonomous bodies; and until something has been worked out with them, and to which they will have agreed, it would probably be looked upon as an undue interference with their autonomous powers. This section 6A provides in subsection 1 that the commission shall coordinate construction and development work in the national capital district in accordance with general plans approved from time to time under the act. That is the general principle, and to carry out that principle the following provisions are made:
(2)	Proposals for the location, erection, alteration or extension of a building or other work by or on behalf of the government of Canada or by any person on lands owned, leased or otherwise controlled by the government of Canada in the national capital district shall be referred to the commission prior to the commencement of the work.
(3)	No building or other work shall be erected, altered or extended by or on behalf of the government of Canada in the national capital district unless the site, location and plans thereof have first been approved by the commission.
(4)	No person shall erect, alter or extend a building or other work on land in the national capital district owned, leased or otherwise controlled by the government of Canada unless the site, location and plans thereof have first been approved by the commission.
(5)	Every person who contravenes or fails to comply with subsection four of this section is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars.
So it is only the activities of the government of Canada, or the placing of buildings on land owned or controlled by the government of Canada, that come, under this section and has to be submitted to the federal district commission for approval. It is only in such cases that section 6A applies. It would seem that the matter has to go before the federal commission before the government can act. The federal commission has full opportunity to investigate it and to make its recommendations. If these recommendations are such that the governor in council feels they should not be complied with, it does not seem unreasonable that he should overrule. But it is only the activities of the government of Canada or the activities carried on on land controlled by the government that are dealt with in these provisions.

speechtext:
This section provides
that the commission shall send to the president of His Majesty's privy council for Canada on or before the first day of September in each year a detailed statement of all its receipts and expenditures up to the last day of March in such year and copies of such statements shall be laid before parliament within the first fourteen days of the next following session thereof. This type of accounting is not very convenient if members of parliament wish to follow the public accounts in order to see that the public is getting value for its money. When you build a railway you know that it costs so much per mile. When you put up a building you can ascertain how much per unit of measurement you will pay for that type of construction. When you come to developments of this type it is difficult for members of the house, or anyone else, from a simple statement of receipts and expenditures, to know whether the public is getting value for its money. Has the commission been in the habit of keeping a working projects cost accounting system so that the various activities of the commission and the expenditures on certain aspects of their work are segregated and analysed and hon. members or any other person interested may determine what certain projects cost or certain parts cost, and so on?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If the hon. member will look at the form of the federal district commission reports which have been issued in the past I think he will find that they are made up in a clear-cut manner, and supply all the information the hon. member has in mind. The act also provides that all expenditures are subject tp the audit of the auditor general in the same manner as other public moneys; and having to keep their accounts so that they may be audited in the same manner as the accounts which are kept for all public moneys, the commission prepares and issues a comprehensive and clear-cut report which indicates what the various projects have cost. The one I hold in my hand is for the year 1942-43. It shows in detail the amount expended on each project. It consists of a whole page of headings. If the hon. member gets these reports I think he will find in them all the information which can be of assistance in coming to a conclusion when further votes are required.

I was in the industrial
relations committee and could not be in the chamber when section 10 was discussed. With the permission of the committee I should like to say a few words on that section. What I have to say affects only Ontario. I am not quarreling with the measure, because it is clear and gives the administration and employers considerable latitude.
In Ontario there is a statutory limitation in respect of the provisions concerning vacations with pay. Under the provisions of the

Ontario Hours of Work and Vacations with Pay Act the soldier who comes back is to be reinstated in his former employment. The arrangement respecting vacation with pay in this province is fixed by statute, and it states that all the employer can pay the soldier going on his vacation is two per cent of his earnings during the time he has been employed. A soldier coming back who has had only ninety days employment and receives vacation with pay would receive only two per cent of the amount he earned in ninety days. The result is that he goes on vacation with a very small amount of money. Many of them want to take only a day or two, but the vacation is mandatory. The result is that they are going on vacations without pay. This condition is peculiar only to Ontario.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942 -REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT

speechtext: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of bill No. 367, to amend the Immigration Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Will the minister make an explanation on the second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
The reason for this bill is that under the Canadian- Citizenship Act which is now in force certain provisions are made which conflict with the provisions of the Immigration Act, and these amendments are necessary to bring the Immigration Act into conformity with the Canadian Citizenship Act. There are no changes of major importance. There is a redrafting of certain provisions to make them clearer, and when we deal with the bill sec-

Immigration Act
tion by section hon. members will see exactly the changes that are made. There is also the elimination of one part of a clause made necessary by the passing of the Canadian Citizenship Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-"Canadian citizen."

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
This proposed amendment
furnishes a new definition of the term "Canadian citizen" to conform with the Canadian Citizenship Act. Until the passing of the Canadian Citizenship Act, the only definition of a Canadian citizen in the statutes was that provided in section 2 of the Immigration Act. By paragraph (b) of this section a British subject who acquired domicile became a Canadian citizen, and such status was relinquished by loss of domicile. Further, a person naturalized also became a Canadian citizen but lost such status on relinquishing domicile. Under section 20 of the Canadian Citizenship Act, a Canadian citizen other than a natural-born Canadian citizen ceases to be a Canadian citizen if he resides outside of Canada for a period of at least six years, unless his certificate of citizenship or passport is endorsed by the officer in charge of a consulate that the person concerned has established that his absence from Canada is of a temporary nature, and that he intends to return to Canada for permanent residence. Since Canadian citizens are admissible to Canada as a matter of right, it is necessary to have the same definition of what constitutes a Canadian citizen in the two acts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: What is the effect of this bill on the British subject who comes to Canada and does not become naturalized under the Canadian Citizenship Act? Under the Immigration Act as it now stands he would become domiciled here after five years for the purposes of the Immigration Act; but now with these amendments he will not do so unless he becomes a Canadian citizen. Is that not right? In other words, we are taking away some of the rights of a British subject from the other parts of the commonwealth.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: No; the position is just as it was, and he acquires domicile in the same manner as before. We are taking away no rights at all from a British subject.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Does the British subject who comes here, let us say, from Australia not have to take out naturalization as a Canadian in order to acquire domicile in Canada under the Immigration Act as it is now proposed to be amended?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: No, he does not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: How can he acquire domicile under the Immigration Act as it is to be amended?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: By five years' residence after legal landing in Canada he acquires domicile and becomes a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Has that always been so?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Surely the minister is confused when he says that he can acquire domicile and yet not become a Canadian citizen. The procedure for becoming a Canadian citizen is a new procedure which has just been enacted this year in the Canadian Citizenship Act. The case I referred to was that of a British subject who comes here from Australia but does not take out naturalization under the Canadian Citizenship Act. You are now changing the Immigration Act so that that man cannot acquire domicile in Canada at any time unless he becomes naturalized.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: By five years' residence in Canada the British subject my hon. friend refers to will acquire domicile now, but does not become a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Under what section?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS FOR PURPOSES OF CONFORMITY WITH CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Under section 2(e) of the Immigration Act, which says:
"domicile" means the place in which a person has his home or in which he resides, or to which he returns as his place of permanent abode, and does not mean the place where he resides for a mere special or temporary purpose.
That is the same definition exactly in the new act. Then paragraph (e)(i) provides:
Canadian domicile can only be acquired, for the purposes of this act, by a person having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein within the meaning of this act.

ponsibility for our own mistake. We have been doing very well to-day, and I think we had better take a breather for a minute or two to discuss some of these estimates. I have one or two .other matters that I wish to discuss on this item because it is the only item on which I think I can discuss what I have in mind. What are the intentions of the department in regard to Ripple Rock? I know that this is a troublesome matter. It is a matter on which a great deal of money has been spent, but I wish to draw the minister's attention to one striking feature in regard to the carrying out of this work which I think has not so far been brought to his attention. Ripple Rock has been the bane of navigators for many long years. When the war commenced it is my information that the United States offered to take out this rock, but for reasons which are commendable we intimated that we would take it out ourselves. We did not say it in those words, but we had that national pride in ourselves which is commendable. Steps were then taken to take out the rock. A model was built at the university of Seattle to test out the tides and the effect of water and the best procedure to be followed in the removal of the rock. Alongside the model was a model constructed for the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission. Since I was down there doing work in regard to the commission I naturally visited the model of Ripple Rock. I said to the man in charge: "Your model of Ripple Rock did not turn out very satisfactorily." I was astounded when he said to me: "Mr. Reid, the trouble was that either the department or the contractor paid no attention whatsoever to the results of our findings." I said: "Why would they have doubts of your findings?" He said: "They have not had much experience in models," and owing to the fact that in the model they had been using small thread the contractor and I think some of our engineers were of the opinion that, because it was thread it did not give a proper recording of what the actual work would be or the dangers of the work when they undertook it.

I should be glad if the minister would make a statement, because I am particularly interested in this matter from several points of view. I think of the United States wanting to take it out, and of Canada refusing. I know great sums of money have been expended there, but surely we are not going tacitly to say to the United States, "Well, you would have taken it out. We thought we could, but we did not." I am going to urge upon the minister that the whole matter be looked into again, in the light of the work done on the model in Seattle. If he investigates I believe he will find that the reports concerning that work were ignored to a large extent. According to the information I have been given, they simply refused to believe that the work on the model would have any bearing on the actual work when it was undertaken. That is my first question. I have one or two to ask, and I should like the indulgence of the committee to allow me to conclude with my questions.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
In my estimates this year there is no item concerning any work on Ripple Rock. The moneys expended were voted in previous years, and I have not with me the complete file concerning the matter, so that to a certain extent I shall have to rely upon my memory in giving the .facts to the committee.
In 1941 naval ships of the United States and Canada were travelling in Seymour Narrows, and there was some discussion as to the possibility of taking out Ripple Rock. The Canadian government did make a war appropriation in the amount of $250,000, as I recall it, to commence this work. We called for tenders, and had a tender from one company who commenced the work; but after expending the $250,000 they had absolutely no success beyond building the scow which was used to try to drill into the rock. They had adopted the method of anchoring the scow in order to drill from it; but the currents and tides were such that they could not do any drilling, so at the end of that season they had to cease work. The next year we again asked who would undertake this work, but could find no one to make a firm bid. We came to an arrangement with one company, I believe it was the British Columbia Bridge and Dredging company, to undertake the work for a fee of $35,000, with this government paying the expenses. This was during the war. They changed the method of dealing with the scow. They put up cables over the straits and tied the scow down in order that the drilling could be carried out. They did drill about 122 holes

Supply-Public Works
from five to six feet deep, and of that number I believe they blew up something around 80 holes. That was only the first layer they were trying to take off. But when it came to dredging this rock which had been blown off. they could not devise any means of clearing it away, and up to the present time no one else has been able to devise any method of dredging even that part which was blown off.
Then we turned around and made an offer to the same company, asking them to give us a definite estimate as to what it would cost to bring the channel down to about thirty-one feet. By that time I may say we had expended $802,825.47, and, if I remember correctly, that company did give us an estimate. They started at $1,200,000, and then it went up to $1,800,000 to complete the work; but they would not give us a guarantee that they could do it even on the firm price they gave us by correspondence. We were prepared to guarantee that over and above that firm price we would be- ready to pay fifty per cent of any additional cost if they could find some insurance company that would guarantee payment of the other fifty per cent. I believe they did look around, not only in this country but all over the world, for some company that would guarantee this payment, but they could not find one.
At last the most rabid proponents of taking away Ripple Rock had to throw up their hands. We are trying to devise some way to help navigation there. On one side of the rock there is a channel of about 1,300 feet and on the other side a channel of five or six hundred feet, and we have had contradictory opinions as to the navigability of those two streams. Actually if the government could have found somebody to undertake the work at an exact or even approximate cost, so that we would know where we were going, we would have had the work done. The best engineers were consulted. My own deputy minister was in Washington and New York to meet their experts, but as yet no method has been found which would promise success. Perhaps if we stayed on the job for another five or six years and spent a million or so a year we might find a way of doing it. but right now the government hesitates to start this work unless we ran find some means which will offer a reasonable hope of success. Speaking from memory, I recall attending meetings where this matter was discussed, and the general opinion seemed to be that the cable system was the best method of stabilizing the scow in order to drill the holes, but that did not succeed.

They did get eighty holes
drilled.

Yes, but to a
depth of only five or six feet; and to get down to thirty-one would mean they would have to repeat that process four or five times. But we could not blow up any more of that rock before clearing out what had been blown up early in the work, and up to the present no one has found a way of doing that. I am told that the cable system was successful at that level, but that they did not have much hope of being able to drill to the required depth. I must say that if my department had succeeded in removing Ripple Rock it would have been extremely proud of the feat; it would have been known all over the world, and the engineers doing that work would have become outstanding men, not only in Canada but elsewhere. Within the last six or seven months I have not received any further requests concerning this work, because it seems to be agreed that unless we can find the proper method we should not be simply spending money. We have put nearly a million dollars into this work to show our good faith. We went all over the place consulting people, trying to get advice and help. No responsible firm seems to wish to undertake this project unless we keep them working without knowing exactly what results we shall get and what will be the cost to the people of Canada. On the other hand, the engineers of my department are still studying the matter to see if they cannot find some way of proceeding. The first method, of simply anchoring the scow, was not a success. The second method, using cables, did bring certain results. Other scientists are studying the rock to see whether by the tunnel process we could not get under the rock and blow it up. The last time I heard any discussion about this matter, someone said the rock was not of the proper formation in order to tunnel under it and blow it up. It has been suggested that cement caissons be used to take the water out. But nobody has said we can get the caissons on this rock to proceed with the work. My advisers have not any method which will assure the government that we would not be spending this money uselessly.
I take it that it is not the minister's intention to drop this project.

I can tell my hon. friend that I have studied the files from the first page to the last, and there is not a single document stating that the United States government would undertake this work. I do not think that would come before the Department of Public Works.
It came before the war committee of the cabinet.

Probably the minister is quite correct when he says his files do not have that entry. Certain ministers made the statement that the offer had been made by the United States government to Canada to take out that rock, because military vessels had to go up through Seymour Narrows on their way to Alaska, and they were afraid of it.
We said no to the United States government, and we were probably right in having said that. But I think pride in our country should make us put forth a great effort to take out that rock, after further survey has been made along the lines I have suggested.

There is no doubt that this :s a difficult engineering problem, but I am afraid that the department has more or less giver, up hope. The minister spoke this afternoon to the effect that if someone could find a way to remove the rock the government would be glad to step in and do it.
But the position is that the government must find the way. We cannot expect a private individual to find a way to remove that rock; it is up to the government to do it; because the situation is so very serious. It has been discussed at considerable length in editorials; this is from an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of February 27 of this year:
Ottawa has been crowding its luck ever since its own royal commission reported in 1931 that the existence of Ripple Rock in the main channel of coastwise shipping through Seymour Narrows constitutes "an ever present possibility of a major accident involving great loss of human life."
It would just take one good wreck to lose probably a good deal more than a million dollars.

Removal of Ripple Rock, dangerous hazard to navigation in Seymour Narrows, has been proved feasible from an engineering standpoint-

-K. W. Morton, district engineer for the Department of Public Works, told the second annual conference of the Pacific Northwest Trade Association here to-day.

May 2 of this year, and this is a statement by one of your own men.

The dispatch goes on to say:
Discussion of the Ripple Rock problem was the initial subject on the agenda after the conference was opened this morning by Lieut-Governor W. C. Woodward.
It goes on to say:
Mr. Morton estimated it would take 34 months' work to remove the top of the rock under the system used by the B.C. Bridge & Dredging Co. This is the company which did all the experimental work that was finally stopped by dominion order when funds ran out.
"The method has proved workable," Mr. Morton said, "most of the problems connected with it have been ironed out. Any of the other more complicated schemes would require a great deal more experimentation and loss of time."
He was referring to the method of anchoring the drill barge over the rock with overhead cables attached to the two shores of the channel.
Cost of the work is estimated at $1,900,000. It is expensive because of the overtime involved for crews and the fact that actual drilling can only be done at ebb tide.
Summarizing the work done, he said 139 holes were drilled, a total of 717 feet. Of these 93 were blasted.
This is the minister's own engineer.
The other 46 were not blasted because of broken drills or other causes. Deepest hole drilled was 15 feet-
Not eight, as the minister said.
-and the average 5-7 feet.
There was complete control over the barge and the experiments definitely showed Ripple Rock can be blasted by this method, he said.
There is the evidence from within the minister's own department. I suggest to him that this scheme should not be dropped.
Hear, hear.
H there were a rock like that in the St. Lawrence it would have been moved decades ago.

But it is out on the Pacific coast, a long way from Ottawa. People out there cannot keep pressing for something to be done about it all the time. This is of vital importance, not only to Canada but to the United States, because the bulk of their shipping to Alaska goes up past that rock. I submit it is a tragedy that this plan should be dropped by the federal government at the present time. There will be a real disaster out there one of these days; possibly a passenger ship will 'be lost, with several hundred lives. Then there will be greater responsibility on the government, if the .work is not proceeded with.
That rock must be moved. The departmental officials cannot just sit here, fold their hands and say, "It's too bad, but we cannot get anything done."

solve the problem, we should find another department or an independent commission or committee which will solve it and remove this menace to the security of our people. Well, you should.

Before this committee considers the items of the chief engineer's branch, I wish to make a few remarks of a general nature on these items.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw the attention of the committee to some items of the engineer's branch which are of particular concern to my constituency. If I have waited until the committee had reached this stage of the discussion on the public works estimates to make my remarks, it is because in my constituency we are not, for the moment at least, specially interested in public buildings which we consider as a luxury. We are primarily interested in the kind of public works that are absolutely essential to our economic development and to the expansion of the two important industries of our district. I shall therefore deal only with the improvement work that has to do with our fishing harbours and with the construction of commercial wharves.
First, as regards the fishing harbours, the sea fisheries of the province of Quebec are mostly concentrated in the constituency of Gaspe, where they form an industry which comes immediately after lumbering. The Gaspe coast being quite precipitous and exposed to the winds which so frequently rage in the gulf of St. Lawrence, it affords no shelter for our fishermen's boats. That is why, if we wish to maintain that industry, we must give special attention to the improvement and construction of easily accessible fishing harbours.
I need not emphasize the important part which our sea fisheries play to-day in the food programme this country has launched with a view to helping the nations devastated by war. To realize that, we merely have to consider the fish exports made through UNRRA. I may add that the Gaspe district has already suffered from the great international crisis which has come to an end with the cessation of hostilities, on account of the participation of this country with the allied nations in efforts to maintain peace, before the last war. The members of this committee no doubt remember the economic sanctions that were imposed against Italy at the time of the Ethiopian war and which entailed for our Gaspe fishermen the loss of the important market they then had in Italy for their dried fish. Moreover, we must recognize the merit of our fishermen who, during the war, did not hesitate to face the ordinary perils of the sea besides the dangers resulting from the incursions of the enemy in the St. Lawrence.

I must add here, better to emphasize the importance of that industry from a national standpoint that the Department of Veterans Affairs is now reestablishing in commercial fisheries the numerous veterans of my district. As every one knows, through legislation introduced in this parliament during the present session, the government is spending huge amounts in order to finance the establishment of our veterans as farmers or fishermen. When we settle a veteran on a farm, the land and buildings he acquires are not so exposed to loss as if the same funds were advanced to him for investment in the fishing boat with which he must earn a living. Besides, in the case of a farm, the veteran may cover any risks by taking out fire or some such insurance. This is however quite impossible to the- veteran engaged in salt water fishing because maritime risks on fishing boats and equipment cannot be covered by any form of insurance now extant. Unless therefore provision is made for the setting up of fishing harbours or safe shelters for our fishermen's boats, I am very much afraid that we shall soon have to cope with the problem of veterans who, having borrowed money from the government to invest in boats, have lost them in the storm before they have had the chance to pay for them. What the government proposes to do in such cases I don't know, but I must point out that so far they have not been provided for by legislation. As an instance of the very real hazards involved, I merely have to mention the case of the small town of Cap des Rosiers, in my constituency, where in a single storm last summer fifteen fishing boats were lost. Each year we sustain similar losses which, unfortunately, are too often coupled with loss of human lives.
The fisherman's task is a hard one; but my Gaspesian fishermen are not seeking wage increases, are not holding out nor ever did hold out the threat of strikes which have brought local economy to a standstill and often threaten the whole national economy. All they ask our government is to give them at least the means to carry on and extend their work.
The fishermen I represent and myself find it hard to understand, that in the transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy, when we are spending huge sums on reconversion, we cannot find the money required, not to reconvert an operating industry, but merely to ensure its survival and expansion. Second, our commercial wharves to which my previous remarks about the importance of our fishing harbours also apply. There again, I submitted to the minister and Department of Public Works a list of urgent projects and I hope that by next year, they will begin to carry out this programme.
We have very important sea ports to which, every year, we ship huge quantities of lumber and pulpwood. As I said earlier, we are almost without rail service; only a fourth rate railroad barely 60 miles in length and a belt road in even worse shape; therefore, as I said on the address in reply to the speech from the throne when parliament was convened, the maritime route is the only means of communication available to our people.
The lumber industry is our main activity and I refer the hom. minister as well as the government to a report on the inventory of the natural resources of the Gaspe area carried out in 1937 by the Quebec government.
I will therefore take the liberty of submitting to the hon. minister a suggestion which I have already put to the officers of his department. Considering the scarcity of lumber resulting from the British Columbia strikes as well as from the house-building programme, I suggest once again that the Minister of Public Works determine alt once the approximate quantity and dimensions of the lumber required for the projects he intends to carry out during the summer of 1947 and immediately place contracts so that he may count on having his order filled by next spring. I might add that if such contracts are handed out this fall, we will be able to secure locally in the Gaspe area a good deal of the lumber needed for these projects and thus reduce the quantities we will require from British Columbia.
I have one more suggestion for the hon. minister; it deals with the dredging near the fishing harbours and commercial docks of my riding. This summer, we experienced a great deal of trouble in having urgent work carried

out due to the fact that the Department of Public Works has placed its dredge at the disposal of two constituencies, Bonaventure and Gaspe, and also because this machinery is so ancient that it is falling apart. As a result, we had to hire outside dredging contractors to do part of the dredging in my constituency; this was done after we had experienced much difficulty and after several of our fishing harbours had been paralysed for a good part of the season owing to the delay in carrying out the necessary dredging operations.
It is therefore necessary and urgent that the Department of Public Works build a dredge for use in Gaspe county and I hope that it will do so shortly.
My third and last suggestion pertains to the lack of personnel at the district engineer's office, at Rimouski. That office is shorthanded in view of the volume of work and of the vast territory it has to cover. As a result, work in our district is delayed, sometimes to a point that it is not carried out during the fiscal year for which the funds have been appropriated. I wish to say a few words, reverting to the Ripple Rock question. I was surprised to hear British Columbia members this afternoon saying that they had been insisting on this work for the last three years. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that every week in my office I have heard representations and have received letters, and I have consulted the best men around me in regard to the work. This afternoon some members made a few remarks which I do not think I should allow to pass without indicating exactly how the government came to its decision.
In my department we had an oustanding engineer, the chief engineer of the department, Mr. Kenneth Cameron, who had been a past president of the Canadian institute of engineers. He is one of the outstanding engineers in the country, has headed that branch of my department for many years, after rising from resident engineer to the top rank, and has now been superannuated. This gentleman had absolutely no interest in giving his minister any advice in which he did not believe. He was honest in the way in which he conducted his work, and I am looking at the hon. member for Carleton when I make that statement, because he knew Mr. Cameron. I am sure the hon. member will agree that Mr. Cameron is one of the outstanding citizens of the country.

He made an investigation in conjunction with my deputy minister. He spent three weeks on the coast and made his final report on the Ripple Rock works. He has now been superannuated, but after his return from that trip he came back to the office for a week or so. Does anyone think I would set aside the report made to me by my chief engineer and accept reports given to me by any outsider who did not know one-tenth as much about the situation as my chief engineer?
What about your own engineer, Mr. Morton, who is right on the coast?

Though I have a great deal of respect for the engineer on the coast, I must point out that he was unoer the direction of Mr. Cameron. Mr. Cameron met him there and they travelled together. But would anyone advise the Minister of Public Works to disregard the advice of his deputy, who is also a civil engineer and an outstanding one, and the advice given by the chief engineer of the department, and say to them, "No, gentlemen; Mr. Morton is out there. What the hon. member read in the clipping from the Vancouver Sun is part of what I said at the outset of my remarks. Certainly; we asked for tenders. They had the specifications and, if they know so much about the work, they ought to be able to put a price on it. Judging by past performances, am I to set aside the report of my chief engineer and say to these gentlemen, "Of course we will give you that contract"; and after spending $1,900,000 without results world you expect me to come back to the hru.e and ask for another $2,000,000? What wiufi oeople say?
You have already got some results.

I think I am being logical in the argument. We decided at the time that if we could get a firm price we would undertake the work. We went farther and said to them, "Though we do not believe in that estimate, if you will find an insurance company who will guarantee fifty per cent of the excess over $1,900,000 we will undertake to pay fifty per cent and your insurance company can give us a guarantee to pay the other fifty per cent." Nobody came forward, however; nobody would undertake it.
Does anyone think we would be justified in spending the people's money at that rate, when I am convinced myself, on the best advice which I could obtain, that they have not found the right method by which to get rid of Ripple Rock? That is our position.
I respect the opinions of those who come from the coast, and hon. members have a right to press their point; but it is not fair to my department to urge me to undertake expenditures of public money when I am not satisfied that we can have the work done. Now that we can come back again for a few minutes to Ripple Rock, because it is still there, may I say that this afternoon I listened with a great degree of interest to the remarks of the hon. members for New Westminster, Vancouver South and Vancouver Centre. I wish to associate myself with all that they have said and, if there is any way of making it stronger, I do so. I think I can say this afternoon that I have probably sailed through Seymour Narrows more often than any other member in the committee, because during the past few years I have sailed through them on a good many occasions. I have seen some' cf the largest steamers which ply on the Pacific coast in these northern waters timing their sailings and their movements to arrive at Seymour Narrows at either high slack or low slack tide. With all the power that they are able to develop, if they should arrive too soon they never attempt to sail through; they anchor. Why? Because, although we have heard this afternoon of many hundreds of feet on this side or on the other side of the rock, a vessel trying to go through these dangerous waters and these tremendous currents runs the danger of being swept irresistibly upon that rock. I know something of how mariners of the north Pacific coast feel every time that they approach Ripple Rock. They approach that rock with a degree of fear and wholesome respect.
I am glad to know that so much money has been spent by the government so far in an attempt to remove Ripple Rock, but I cannot quite understand some of the remarks which the minister made this afternoon. One of the difficulties which seem to baffle them at the present moment is how to clear the top of the rock after blasting operations have taken place. I can hardly visualize that difficulty when I know something of the force of the explosives used. If it does not blow the rock completely away from the surface I can tell the minister that if there are chunks of rock on the top as big as this desk the tides and currents will sweep them off.
They are probably bigger than that.

If
they are bigger than that I do not think their

speechtext:
