The point is that we have spent a great amount of money so far, and I do not for one moment
think we are justified now in throwing up our hands and saying that, because our engineers cannot find a satisfactory way to remove the rock, it will have to stay there. I know how 'the minister feels, that if he goes ahead and spends so many millions of dollars and 'fails, his department will be censured, but I can assure the minister that his department will be censured far more if we lose a large vessel on that rock, with heavy loss of life; and that is likely to happen any moment, even while I am speaking. It may happen at any time.
Certainly; and it could have happened in the past hundred and fifty years.

It was stated here this afternoon that the last vessel to suffer damage on the rock was a government vessel, and that the delicate instruments on that vessel, worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, were absolutely ruined. So my contention is that if our Canadian engineers have failed we should call in the engineers of some other country.

We did. My deputy spent a good deal of time consulting the best engineers in New York and Washington, the best engineers on that kind of work in the United States, and their report agreed with the report I received from my own officials. We are not all engineers, you know.
The last method adopted was to string a cable, at tremendous expense to the country.
What about the other methods? Did you study them? Did you study the tunneling method?
Yes; I know the methods they have been trying to follow. The overhead cable method was the most successful so far. Why was the cable taken down?

I gave that
answer a moment ago. Ten feet of water flows continually over this rock. In addition to that, we were to drill another twenty-one or twenty-two feet. We did start drilling so many holes at the first level of five feet. That was the average; perhaps it may have been six feet, and they drilled as many holes as they could. Then they filled the holes with dynamite or some explosive, and tried to explode it. Two-thirds were blown up, say eighty holes out of 120. Ripple Rock is not just a peak of rock coming up in the middle of the water. It spreads around, and the rock that was blown off spread over the
Supply-Public Works

rest of it. The contractors tried to remove the loose rock but had no success, and they could not go on and drill a second level of five or six or seven feet without removing the first rock. Then the deeper they went, to drill the harder it became to keep the barge and scow sufficiently stable that the drills would not be broken. That was the second method. The first was to anchor the scow and barge, but that did not succeed at all.
I know.
The first project cost us around $350,000, and the second one, nearly $500,000, and we have had no success.
Some success.

A third method was suggested, that of tunneling,-but we were advised against it. I am no expert; I am only repeating what I have heard when this matter has been discussed. We were told that ;he rock formation would, not permit of :unneling and having the rock blown up. A fourth method suggested, which would be a costly one .and in one connection with which no one could assure us of success, would be by dropping cement caissons on the rock, taking out the water and then trying to drill. All these ideas came from engineers; they did not come from laymen, and in each case the objections were such that, after spending $800,000, I did not feel I could recommend to the government that we proceed farther unless I could be convinced by the experts that it was feasible. We have consulted engineers in the United States. Hon. members have said the government of the United States told us they would do the work, but I have been dealing with this question for nearly four years and it has not come to my knowledge yet that the United States government asked to be allowed to proceed with the work. There is a lot of talk about doing this and doing that, but when you Come down to the facts there is nothing on the file that would show that any other government would undertake this work, or that they had better engineers than we have in our own country.

From all I can gather, the last method adopted, using the overhead cable, did bring a certain amount of success. The minister himself admits that a certain number of holes were dtrilled and blasted. What I cannot understand is why, after all that expenditure and all the risk of life and limb in stringing that overhead cable, it was not left there. Why take it down?
fMr. A. Fournier.]

Because we could not get a price from anybody to complete the work by the cable method. As I said, I have dealt with this matter for nearly four years. It was the most important thing I had in my mind in connection with the department, because we were anxious to make a success of it. Just imagine; if our department could have succeeded in that work-I am repeating what I have said previously- our engineers would have become great men amongst the engineers on this continent. When we tried last fall to get a firm price for the work, no firm prices were given to us. We had one estimate of $1,800,000 or $1,900,000, but there was no guarantee that they would do the work for that amount, any more than they did the work for the $250,000 or $300,000 we paid in. the first place, and we asked for a guarantee. They could not find anybody even .to guarantee fifty per cent of the excess over the estimate of about $1,900,000.

Even yet the minister does not answer my question. We had a cable strung across a given area at tremendous expense. It would not have hurt the department to leave that cable there even yet, until you finally decided whether or not you were going to use the cable method again. It may be that you will have to come back to the cable.
I can give you the reason in a minute if you want it.

Pardon me; the minister has spoken enough. You may have to go back to the cable method) yet, and all I want to know is, why did you take down the cable before you were absolutely sure that method could not be used?

When we put up the cables we had reports that they were dangerous to navigation. Opinion was divided even in connection with stringing up those cables across the rock. When we were convinced that we could not proceed by the cable method we did not think we should hinder navigation by allowing those cables to remain over the straits.

I am not satisfied that navigation was hindered. Navigation went on all the time. The minister can wave his hand; but, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre said, Ripple Rock is too far from Ottawa; that is the whole trouble. I would repeat what the hon. member for Vancouver South said, that if it had been, in the St. Lawrence river they would have made greater attempts to remove it than have so far been made. Let the govern-

Supply-Public Works
ment go ahead and spend money without asking for too many guarantees that this will be done or that will succeed.

Would you suggest that in dealing with public works I should go ahead and give out work without getting firm prices; that I should spend the money of the taxpaying public of Canada without any guarantee that the work will be completed for the money we pay out? Do you think that would be the proper way to administer the Department of Public Works? Do you think I could rise in this house and defend that policy; that I could say, "All right; you want work out in British 'Columbia. We don't care what the cost is. We don't care if you can do the work. We are just going to spend the money of the people." Do you think that sort of policy would be upheld in this house? Do you think I could rise in my place and defend a policy of that kind? If that sort of policy were to be adopted I probably would not be long in this government, because I do not believe it would be good government.
That is exactly what the minister has been doing up to now.
May I ask a question?
I have the floor.
You are afraid to answer a question?

The minister has expended a good many hundred thousand dollars on a worth-while experiment, and we are asking that the experimentation proceed. I think that is fair. The minister has been prosecuting this work, and there has been no criticism of his department from any source for having done so. His department is worthy of commendation, because he has tried to do something. But we maintain that this is not the time to fold up and say, "We give up, because Ripple Rock is too large for us." I still feel there are engineers in this country-and if Canadian engineers cannot do it, others can-
(Name them.

That is not my place. It is not for hon. members to find a solution; it is for the government to find one. The warning still holds good that some day there will be a disaster at Ripple Rock, and it will reflect upon the government, if this work is not carried out.

I wish to tell the minister that it appears that Ripple Rock is a considerable item. I was not in the chamber when the discussion began, so that to that extent I am under a handicap because I do not know what other members have said.
I am not an engineer and I know nothing about Ripple Rock, except that I have heard it is there and is dangerous. I also know it is a live question in British Columbia. I listened to what the minister said about what had already been done in attempting to remove this obstruction to navigation. I believe there was considerable merit in the stand he took, provided that the matter is not allowed to drop because of the difficulties now being met. If the Department of Public Works will give a guarantee to put an. item in the estimates to keep on with this work-and I am not suggesting that the minister should keep on with a method that has not proved successful-but if he will give the assurance that attempts will be made to remove the danger, that is all we are entitled to ask. He has said that he would be criticized if he spent money on this without obtaining results. He would be criticized, and criticized from this side of the house.
That has been the practice in parliament, and we should not press him to undertake work where he is satisfied that he will not succeed. But no matter how difficult it is, the removal of Ripple Rock is of great importance. In the light of the engineering feats which have been accomplished in the world in the last few years, surely we are not going to allow ourselves to be baffled by this situation. The minister should give the committee an undertaking that every effort will be continued for. the removal of Ripple Rock. The minister has said that engineers had been consulted in New York, but I suggest that they could be brought on the scene, and their opinions obtained. When that is done I am sure some means will be found for removing the rock. If large expenditures are undertaken, but without success, I will assure the minister that so far as I am concerned I shall support him if the question is brought dp in the house.
I should like to take a few minutes to make a few general remarks on the subject now being discussed, because it relates to the fishing industry, an industry which I am sure-
Order. We are discussing the item for the chief engineer's branch.

I wish to speak about wharves and dredging, which would come under this item. The hon. member for Gaspe touched upon these two subjects, and since they are related to the fishing industry I believe I am entitled to speak. I would not speak at all at this time if I had thought all hon. members had understood what was said by the hon. member for Gaspe. He has expressed facts which I would urge in connection with the fishing population, and the problems he has set out are, I believe, identical with those of the fishing population in -my constituency in New Brunswick, and in the maritime provinces generally.
All hon. members realize that during the war many projects had to be abandoned. However, now that we are about to enter the period of reconstruction, let me point out to the Minister of Public Works that we are in need of many improvements and many facilities to promote the fishing industry in the maritime provinces. I should hope that when he considers the problems pointed out by the hon. member for Gaspe, and the promise he made to the hon. member, he would also keep my section of New Brunswick in mind, because we have similar problems. There is a certain attitude which I do not approve in the Department of Public Works with reference to new undertakings. I do not blame the officials. But on occasions when I have approached them respecting the construction of new projects I have always been told that it was impossible because the revenue at the point in question was not sufficient to warrant the expenditure. I do not blame the officials because they are following a policy. But I think the policy is wrong. I do not think the necessity for a certain public work should be gauged by the actual revenue at that point. That should not be the criterion. I think what should also be considered is the potential revenue that might be derived if proper fac-ities were provided.
Hear, hear.

The hon.
member says "hear, hear" and I presume that members from the west would say the same. The maritime provinces, during the last thirty or forty years when great developments were taking place in other parts of the country in the matter of railways and canals, did not suggest that the actual revenue to be derived from the- start of such construction should be considered, but the potential revenue if the great open spaces were opened up and developed, and we hope that the same policy will be applied to the maritimes.

Supply-Public Works
Our most important industry in the mari-times is the fishing industry, and I want to emphasize that public works are linked with the success of our most important industry. We admit that in the maritimes we do not possess great wealth. As I look toward the west I see the great forest resources of British Columbia, that great wheat basket in the western plains, the rich forest and mining resources of Quebec and Ontario. But in the maritimes we do not possess great natural resources. Therefore our most important industry, the fishing industry, should be developed to the hilt. This cannot be done unless the fisherman has adequate facilities and the protection which he needs. I have heard in this house many a recital of the hardships of the farmers of the west and other parts of this dominion. I am not acquainted,
I regret to say, although I hope to be some day, with conditions in1'the west. I know, however, that the farmer has a hard life. But it is nothing compared with that of the fisherman. There is no comparison whatever between the two. The fisherman starts out for two or three weeks fishing in the treacherous waters of the north Atlantic, never knowing whether he will return to his family. When he does return he has not the facilities, the wharves and breakwaters, to approach the shore and protect his boat and gear. The farmer's hardships are nothing compared with those of the fisherman.
Let us look forward to what the fishing industry might be if proper facilities were provided. We must remember also that the youth of to-day will not stand for the hardships of the pioneers of yesterday. He wants something better than his forefathers had and which he knows he should get. If we really want our young men to take up fishing as a vocation we have to give them the facilities which they should have. Study the figures of the returns which the fisherman gets in normal times, not the higher prices they are getting now, and the damages sometimes running into hundreds of dollars, wiping out the earnings of a whole year's work or two years which he sometimes suffers when his boat is smashed against the shore because of lack of proper protection. I know communities which have been in existence for over a hundred years in the northern part of New Brunswick and where fishing has been the mainstay of the people, which still lack these facilities. I do not blame the minister and his officials. It is the policy which has been followed for years that is to blame.
The other day I asked for a little improvement on a wharf. The capital expenditure to improve it would be about $800, and the 63260-292J
annual maintenance, $200. The officials of this department pointed out to me that the revenue was not sufficient. I admitted it. But that wharf was not built for revenue purposes. It was built to accommodate the fishermen who go out into the ocean and produce wealth for this country running into thousands of dollars-untold wealth if they were only provided with proper facilities. I also pointed out that over this same wharf $350,000 worth of sea products was handled, all of which went as a contribution to the country's wealth. It helped to support a number of people; it provided revenue for our railways. Therefore I say that the actual revenue of the wharf should not be the criterion as to whether an expenditure should be made for improvements. We should rather look forward and consider how such improvements might develop the fishing industry.
I am told, and I have it for a certainty, that a number of firms are willing to come and establish themselves in our fishing communities if they can be assured that the fishermen will have proper landing facilities so that these firms can be guaranteed a steady supply. Remember that the fishing industry has changed considerably in the last few years, and therefore we must change our policy to meet those changing conditions.
I hope the Minister of Public Works will be as generous in dealing with these problems in the maritimes as his predecessor in office was, even to other parts of the dominion. We are only asking for the maritimes what we are entitled to. We do not ask for works to be constructed just for the sake of spending money. If I ever looked upon a wharf and thought I had asked for money to be spent on it just for the sake of spending money I would be ashamed and think that wharf was a monument to false judgment on my part. We are asking only what we are entitled to. I know it has been impossible for the department to undertake certain public works during the past five or six years, but from now on let it study our problems in the mari-times so that we will get our just share of assistance.

I was interested in the discussion that took place this afternoon in connection with Ripple Rock. I am not going to transgress the rules by discussing that question, but it was a matter of interest to me to note the manner in which the members from the Pacific coast advanced their claim for expenditures.
There is one item in which I am particularly interested and which I believe will come under this vote. It is a- problem for the engineering branch of the Department of Public Works, and the matter is one that I have brought to the attention of the department and of the minister on more than one
occasion. I refer to the situation that exists at Devil's Island. This is a lonely spot about seven miles by sea from the docks of Halifax city and half a mile from the shores of eastern passage, a small fishing and farming hamlet on, the east mainland, where a tiny wedge of slate rock forced its way above the swelling tides and rolling breakers of the Atlantic. In the past, I admit, a considerable amount of money has been spent in connection with breakwaters, but unfortunately it has not provided the protection which is required to enable the fishermen to carry on their pursuits as such.
I cannot do better, in attempting to describe this locality, than to quote the words of Miss May C. O'Regan. She says:
Remote, grim and desolate, devoid of trees, swept by winds which carry off the sparse soil, the tiny dot just outside the entrance to Halifax harbour, to-day merits the name of Devil's Island even more than it did four generations ago when a little colony of fishermen and pilots settled there to be near the sources of their living.
I emphasize those words, "swept by winds." I am asking the Minister of Public Works to be good enough to go into this matter more fully than apparently he has done in the past. It is extremely difficult and sometimes impossible to get medical help to this island. The district can be serviced) by planes, but at certain times it is impossible to land) either from a boat or from a plane, and we would be pleased if the minister would give us some assurance that this matter will be looked into.
Perhaps a bridge.

If the minister would give us the assurance of a bridge we would be satisfied, but I am not asking for unreasonable things. I am simply asking him to go into the question of providing a breakwater which will serve the purpose. I believe I have given him in the past practically all the information that would be helpful in dealing with this problem, but if he feels that it would cost too much money to erect and maintain a breakwater on the island so as to afford) the protection which the people who live there desire, then I would ask him to present to the government, for their consideration, a scheme whereby there might be provided some place on the mainland where these people can be properly housed and given the attention which we expect human beings to receive in these modem days.
Carried.

No, it is not carried. It is a human need I am talking about. I do not know how closely the minister has followed the doings of the lightkeepers and those who
Supply-Public Works

dwell in these remote places along our Atlantic coast, but if he has not been in touch with the situation there, I suggest to him that he read an interesting book written by E. M. Robertson, wife of the lightkeeper at one of the lighthouses on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia. If he will do this he will realize something of the hardships with which these people have to put up day in and day out, particularly during stormy seasons. I could dwell at great length in describing their hardships, but I will not make myself unpopular at this late hour by taking up more of the time of the committee, though it is an important question and I am making a plea for the satisfaction of a crying human need. I expect a little more consideration than simply to have the minister say that when the house closes he will read the book. It is not the book that I am talking about; I am talking about the plight of the people on Devil's Island. I am asking whether favourable consideration could not be given to the construction of a suitable breakwater which would meet the requirements of these people, or, if not that their problem be taken into consideration and a decision made as to the best scheme to follow. If it is not possible to build or repair the breakwater, then some scheme should be devised to bring these people to the mainland so that they may enijoy the privilege which the minister and the rest of us enjoy in these modern times.

I wish to apologize if the hon. member thinks I was treating his suggestions lightly. I listened most attentively to what the hon. gentleman said, and I was trying to recall the numerous cases which were brought to my attention in my office by other hon. members. I am giving attention to the particular case he has mentioned and I shall continue to do so. I am sorry if I offended him.

I wish to thauK the minister
for adopting a more serious tone with respect to this matter.

Item agreed to.

Chief engineer's branch-Dredging-
800. Ontario and Quebec, $583,840.

Since I am one of the few members present from Ontario and since I have not the problem of rocks and harbours I should like to say a few words on a drainage scheme, known as Running creek. This Running creek is a small offshoot from the St. Clair river. It leaves the river in an unusual way. Most creeks run into the river, but this particular creek near the town of Wallaceburg leaves the river, goes across the country, meets with another creek at the town of Wallaceburg and then finds its way down to lake St. Clair.
In 1965 the Department of Public Works did dredge running creeks. They did it in those days to help out the sugar beet industry. At that time they inaugurated the sugar beet industry in that section of the country and a factory was built at Wallaceburg. That was before the advent of good roads, and in order to assist the farmers who lived six or eight miles out to get their sugar beets into the factory the department dredged that creek. The creek is now filled up. If it were dredged it would serve two purposes. In the first place, that section of the country consists of low-lying land; we call it Little Holland. You pretty nearly have to wear your wooden shoes when you go there, particularly after a rainstorm. There are two or three pumping works there where they have to pump water off the land into this particular creek. Of course they have to pay a municipal tax for that purpose. It was under a municipal scheme.
If the dredging were done it would provide better health services for Wallaceburg, because the little creek water runs for a good many miles before it comes to that town. It runs through several little towns and the sewage disposal is not very well taken care of. In the summer time, around Wallaceburg the water becomes quite stagnant in Running creek. When it was dredged out a number of years ago the blue water left the St. Clair river and came down to the Skey river. You could trace it all the way into the town of Wallaceburg, and the other water was washed away and the town kept healthy. At the present time it is filled up. Wallaceburg is one of the most progressive little towns in western Ontario. Its citizens are all cooperatively-minded, they all work together for the good of their town. They are very much interested in this matter at the present time and hope that we can get the Department of Public Works interested in carrying out that dredging scheme. I believe last fall the engineers got their own local engineer and

Supply-Public Works
he made a survey of it. I believe there will be two or three townships interested in it.
I notice in the estimates that there are $200,000 more allocated to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec than was the case last year. That would be about $100,000 each.
I was wondering whether it would be possible for the Department of Public Works to assist municipal councils in a drainage scheme of this kind, particularly when the department is not taking care of their own local waters, but is taking care of international waters which leave the river and go across the country.

I shall have my engineers report on the case the hon. member has just submitted. The hon. member understands that if it is completely a drainage project we do not contribute to that, but I shall see what we can do about it.
It is drainage, but the water is international water which leaves the river. I thought we would have to take care of international waters.
We have no estimates at all for drainage purposes; I am sorry. We are discussing item 300. We have no money for drainage purposes under this item, nor under any item.

Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch-Dredging-
SOI. Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories, $269,550.

I had intended telling the minister about some of the hazards of shipping on lake Winnipeg and the Red river, up to the harbour of Winnipeg, but since the hour is late I shall refrain from doing so. I want the minister to know that I am going to take these matters up with him, and I hope he will give me an attentive ear. Are the dredges on lake Winnipeg in full operation now, or are they still operating on the war schedule?
My information is that we are operating at full time in Manitoba.

Can the minister tell me what they are doing at Warren's Landing to straighten the channel there? The department made a survey there last year and put in new range lines. If the minister has not the information now, perhaps he could let me have it later.
I shall send it over to the hon. member.

I do not know just how big a field dredging takes in. We do not have a great deal of that work in Saskatchewan, although I believe there is some work along that line that could be done. I was absent this afternoon in the industrial relations committee when the bill to beautify Ottawa was passed, which I would have opposed. Could the minister possibly find an appropriation somewhere to do a little dredging in the Swift Current river. We need a swimming-pool there which would help us out quite a bit.

Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch-Dredging
S02. British Columbia and Yukon, $386,080.

There is just one point I should like to bring up. I do not wish to criticize or to raise the devil too much with the minister because I see he has an item in here for Hazelton; therefore I shall go fairly easily.
That has been voted.

I am not going to speak on that. I should like to deal with dredging at Dalketla slough. I received a letter from the district engineer, Mr. K. W. Morton, of New Westminster, with an outline of the projects contemplated for the Pacific coast, and in that was $301,950 for a breakwater at Wiah Point. I do not see that included in the estimates here. Has it been dropped?

I am informed that the estimates which were given to the hon. member were probably a post-war and timing project. They are not in these estimates. I shall look up the item mentioned by the hon. member and see what can be done about it, but not at this session.

Under these contemplated post-war projects, I should like to bring in this matter; along with Wiah Point, dredging should be done at the village of Massett, so that the fishermen can go over and live in that district. It is important to the fishermen who go out on long-line trawling in that area. It would build up the Queen Charlotte islands. It is a marvellous harbour if it was improved.

I hesitate to rise and urge a complaint against another British Columbia constituency, particularly since that constituency is represented by an hon. member on the other side of the house; but all the filth from the Fraser valley is brought down and deposited in my constituency. I want it removed. The silt from the Fraser river comes down and is filling up the harbours of Nanaimo, Ladysmith and Chemainus;
Supply-Public Works

the harbours in the Gulf islands; Sidney; the great harbour of Victoria-about which I shall have something to say in a moment- and the entrance of the San Juan river.
First. I want to deal with the entrance of the San Juan river. That is the very centre of an extensive logging country. Every year hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of logs are exported through that harbour. The entrance of the harbour leading to Port Renfrew is silting up to such an extent that the tugs of the Malahat Logging Company and the Hemmingsen-Cameron Logging Company are having the greatest difficulty in getting their logs over that bar. I suggest that one thing we need in this country at the present time is lumber; and if from the heart of the lumber country we cannot export our logs to the mills on the mainland because of a lack of dredges, then this department must make a strenuous effort to provide the necessary dredges so that these logs can be exported.
That condition exists not only on the southern coast of Vancouver island but also on the eastern coast, at those other harbours I mentioned:	Nanaimo, Ladysmith and
Chemainus, where the big mills of the Arictoria Lumber Company are situated, and at the harbour of Sidney, where we have ferries running not only from the mainland of British Columbia but also from the United States. All those harbours are silting up. All those harbours demand immediately the dredging operations they were denied during the war years, and one can understand why they were denied that work. A great deal of work is now needed, not only to make up for what should have been done during the war years, but in order to get the lumber from Vancouver island out to the mills, and to the reconstruction projects all over Canada.
I want to say one word about the harbour of Victoria, which is also silting up. As the minister no doubt knows, recommendations have been made as to the purchase of Riffett docks and the development of what is known as fishermen's harbour in Victoria. I believe the minister has this question under consideration. I should like to ask the minister what is being done and how far the negotiations have proceeded in connection with those two projects in the harbour of Victoria. I should like also to have the minister to tell us how many dredges we have on the Pacific coast. I listened with amazement a few minutes ago to references to dredge No. 11, No. 12, No. 13, No. 14, No. 15, No. 16 and No. 17 being employed on the Atlantic coast. I

do not believe we have anything like that number on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before the minister replies, may I tell my hon. friend that the committee will note with great appreciation this "war of the Georges."
I should like an answer to my question.

I am sorry, but under item 302 my hon. friend is discussing matters which come under item 321, where he will see:
Victoria-toward dredging, $100,000.
Victoria-fishing harbourage, $67,000.
The contract for the fishing harbour has not yet been given out, but I understand that we are calling for tenders in the very near future.
The other question was as to how many dredges we have on the Pacific coast. We have four dredges, two tugs, six scows, two motor boats, sixty-four pontoons and one pile-driver barge.
I am afraid the motor boats will not do much dredging, will they?
I do not know. I am no expert, but they might help.
What about Riffett wharf at Victoria? What is the position of those negotiations?

I am sorry I
have not the information here, but I shall let my hon. friend know. I shall send a request to the official to prepare a report and shall give my hon. friend the information.

Negotiations have been
under way for some time, and that is all linked up with the development of the harbour at Victoria and the dredging necessary there.

We have two
items covering what the hon. gentleman has asked. We are now calling for tenders as to the first item, and we are negotiating in regard to the fishing harbour. That is about all the information I have now, unless I look over the file.

Surely the minister can
tell me how far those negotiations have gone. We have been talking about this matter for the past three years; it has been actively discussed in all the newspapers month after month.

The hon. gentleman will find those two items concerning Victoria on page 46 of the estimates under

Supply-Public Works
item 321. I can read what notes I have here and give him the information they contain as to this item of fishing harbourage. This item is to provide for dredging and the construction of an approach landing pier, gangway and floats. Proposed work is urgently required to accommodate an additional 220 fishing boats which have no permanent place to moor at present. The proposed work includes the removal of approximately 22,000 cubic yards of gravel, silt and so on; constructing main float sixteen feet by 1,770 feet; constructing eight floats ten feet by 200 feet with moorings, constructing approach landing pier and gangway. The estimated cost for the removal of 22,000 cubic yards of gravel at eighty cents per cubic yard is $17,600; for floats, gangway and pier, $48,958; for inspection, advertising and contingencies, $442, making a total of $67,000 for that one item. We are not on the right item. I wonder if the hon. member would let this item pass and when we get to item 321-

No, it is not carried at the
present time. We cannot get away without saying something about what the hon. member for Nanaimo said about the Fraser river. It was nice that he said it with a smile, but that smile will not appear on Hansard. It was a kind of slur about what the Fraser river brings down. From what I know about his riding-and I lived there for many years- it is just what his riding needs.
May I suggest that the Nanaimo riding needs little free silt.

Of course Nanaimo has deteriorated since I left there-because I did happen to live there for a certain number of years. But to keep the record clear, he knows very well that what the Fraser river brings down does not go farther than the middle of the gulf. You can see the line of demarcation. But it is just too bad it does not go any farther.
Having disposed of that, 1 should like to speak about something more practical in connection with dredges. We have operating on the Fraser river two dredges. It was news to me that there were four of them, when the minister said so a minute ago. But the two dredges operating on the Fraser river-and I think sometimes in Nanaimo and sometimes at Victoria-are not sufficient at all for the work in British Columbia.
Those dredges are forty-five or fifty years old, and they are inadequate. I should like the minister seriously to tell hon. members from
British Columbia-not myself particularly, because we are all interested in the matter- when we are to have modern dredges, fit and able to keep up with the work required. I know he was presented with a large brief by the New Westminster board of trade, and they set out just what industry's position was in regard to water transportation and dredging requirements. I am not going to read into the record what these firms have said, because it will take too much time. But if the minister has read it-and I hope he has-he .will realize that there is great need for modern dredges for the Fraser river.
During the period of the war a great deal of work was done by these dredges, with the result that siltation took place on the river. In many places industries were entirely blocked because, as is well known, thousands of tons of fine silt or sand come down the Fraser river every year, and are deposited at various places along the bank. If this is not taken out this year, twice as much will have to be taken out next year. Many places have become almost impassable for boats, so far as reaching the wharves is concerned.
We are years behind the time, and I would ask the minister to give some assurance that the matter of new dredges will be looked into and considered seriously-not just by saying, "Oh, well, after the session is over we will give the matter some consideration." Appeals have been made to him for the last three or four years, and we were told that the war was on. But, as the hon. member for Nanaimo has said, the war is now over, and we want to cash in by getting some results.
I would appreciate it if the minister would give us some assurance as to what will be done in the matter of dredges. I would refer, too, to the railway bridge across the Fraser river at New Westminster. Siltation has been taking place until it has become an expensive item to keep that part of the river dredged. This year it was suggested that a model be set up by the national research council, with a view to finding out what steps could or should be taken to keep that portion of the river free from silting up. It has become so serious that it would be necessary to keep a dredge working continuously at that one spot, if satisfactory results were to be obtained.
I do not know whether the minister has seen the model, but one of his engineers took me to see it in operation. I suggest that that model is in the wrong place. No man who has seen the Fraser river only once, and then has returned to Ottawa and attempts to carry out his experiments three thousand miles away,
Supply-Public Works

can operate successfully. 1 suggest 'that if the minister has any say at all, so far as ithe national research council is concerned, he should ask that this model and the experimentation be taken out to British Columbia, so that the work could be carried on more effectively than it can be done here, so fax from the coast.
Mr. CRU1CKSHANK: It being so close to seven o'clock, may I call it seven o'clock?
The hon. member for Kootenay West.
I wish-
I should have an answer in connection with this matter of dredging. Monday morning it will be forgotten.
We will bring it up again.

I have hadl a discussion about, not four new dredges, but one new dredge on the coast. I thought that would be a good start. We are looking into the matter and, without giving a definite assurance, I may tell the hon. member 'that we will consider most seriously the construction of a new dredge.
As to the silt near the bridge, and the model mentioned, I must admit I have not seen the model.
It does not mean anything, anyway.

I might ask the national research council if they would send the model to British Columbia.
Mr. GIBS'ON (Comox-Alberni): It is made out of plasticine.

I am not very well acquainted with the model, or the condition of silt under the bridge. But I shall have my engineer, who showed the hon. member the model, see if it can be sent out, to help work out there.
